intro: Long before anyone kept a diary in the modern sense, someone kept a timetable. In 2013 a French-Egyptian mission led by Pierre Tallet, working with Gregory Marouard and Sayed Mahfouz at Wadi al-Jarf, an Old Kingdom harbour on the Gulf of Suez about 20–25 km south of modern Zafarana, found several hundred fragments of papyrus jammed into the rubble at the mouths of two storage galleries, G1 and G2. They are the oldest inscribed papyri yet found in Egypt, and one of them carries the date 'the year after the 13th cattle count' of King Khufu: the last known year of the king who built the Great Pyramid. The centre of this prologue is the inspector Merer, a mid-level official whose team of roughly forty men (some early reports said about 200) spent part of that year moving fine white limestone by boat from the quarries of Tura, on the east bank of the Nile, to Akhet-Khufu, the 'Horizon of Khufu' — the Great Pyramid at Giza. His record is laid out like a ruled ledger: each day gets two columns, one for what the team did, one for where it slept, with red lines dividing the ten-day weeks. It is not a diary of feelings. It is something older and plainer: a working man's account of where he was on each day, kept because the state wanted to know. This chapter is honest about its genre. Every 'eye' here is a log, an account sheet or an official inscription, not a personal diary, and the form tags say so. Merer's logbook (Papyrus Jarf A and B, published by Tallet in 2017) is the best preserved. Around it sit the much more fragmentary logbooks published in 2021 (Jarf C, D, E, F and Aa), including the record associated with the scribe Dedi, who oversaw all four sections of the same team; and the tabulated account papyri (Jarf G to L) in which harbour scribes tallied grain and bread arriving from the provinces, in red and black ink. The great noble Ankhhaf, Khufu's half-brother, appears only as Merer saw him: a name and a title at a canal-side office. Read together they give a rare double view of the pyramid age: from the river deck, where a crew shuttles blocks between quarry and building site two or three times every ten days during the flood, and from the storeroom, where someone counts the sacks that feed them. The archive was buried, it seems, as the harbour was shut down at the end of Khufu's reign, and lay untouched for some four and a half thousand years. In July 2016 parts of it went on public display for the first time at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. What these documents do not tell us is just as important. They name no hardships, no opinions, no prayers. Merer never says what he thought of the pyramid. But they prove that the urge to set down 'today we did this, tonight we slept there' is as old as monumental building itself — the root from which the later diaries in this book grow.

title: Written in the Stars: Babylon Watches Alexander

intro: Every night for some six hundred years, scholars attached to Esagila, the great temple of Marduk in Babylon, went up to watch the sky and wrote down what they saw: where the moon stood against the stars, which planets had risen, whether clouds hid everything. At the end of each entry, and at the end of each month, they added the things that happened on the ground — the price of barley and dates, the height of the Euphrates, fires, plagues, the movements of kings. Modern scholars call these tablets the Astronomical Diaries. They were not personal diaries; no single scribe signs them, and the observations were later copied and compiled. But they are dated to the night, written within days or weeks of the events, and kept by people who had no stake in flattering a Macedonian king. That makes them the closest thing to a same-day eyewitness record that survives for Alexander the Great. Two of these tablets anchor this chapter. One, in the British Museum (BM 36761 with its join BM 36390), covers the sixth and seventh Babylonian months of 331 BC: a total eclipse of the moon on 20 September, panic in the Persian camp, the battle on 1 October that the Greeks called Gaugamela, the flight of Darius III, messages promising the restoration of Esagila, and Alexander — called by the scribe 'king of the world' — at the gates of Babylon around 21 October. The other (BM 45962) covers the second month of 323 BC. Between a note that Mercury stood above Saturn and a run of cloudy nights, it records, in two words of Akkadian, that the king died. Set against those clay tablets are the Greek and Roman accounts most readers know. Almost all of them are late. Arrian, Plutarch, Diodorus and Curtius Rufus wrote between about 270 and 450 years after the events, compiling earlier works that are now lost: the court historian Callisthenes, the engineer Aristobulus, King Ptolemy of Egypt, and a day-book of Alexander's last illness called the Royal Ephemerides (Royal Journal), which survives only in quotation and whose authenticity is still argued. This chapter treats those later writers honestly as what they are — careful or colourful historians, not eyewitnesses — and flags every lost source as known only through them. The honest record here is therefore mostly logs, chronicles and later histories, not diaries in the modern sense; the 'form' of each eye says which. The Babylonian scribes appear as institutional eyes, named by role. There is no Persian eye at all. The administrative clay archives of Persepolis, which might have shown the empire from the inside, stop generations earlier: the Fortification tablets run from 509 to the 490s BC and the Treasury tablets to the 450s. Ironically, the fire Alexander set at Persepolis in 330 BC helped bury and preserve those older archives, so the empire speaks in this chapter only through its conquerors and its Babylonian subjects. What makes these eyes worth setting side by side is how differently they saw the same weeks. The Greek writ

intro: There is no diary of the last days of Pompeii. Nobody in the buried towns kept one that survived, and the people who saw Vesuvius erupt in AD 79 left us, in all, one eyewitness account: two letters written by Pliny the Younger to the historian Tacitus about twenty-seven years afterwards. This chapter is therefore built differently from the others. It sets that single eyewitness beside the last dated words of the towns themselves — receipts, loan contracts, sworn oaths and court pledges on wax tablets, a charcoal scrawl and the election notices on the walls — and beside the later writers who shaped how the disaster was remembered. The documents have a strange power precisely because they are not about the eruption. A banker in Pompeii pays the town for a tax contract; a woman collects her auction money; a grain dealer at Puteoli pledges his wheat and swears by the emperor's guardian spirit; a young woman in Herculaneum goes to law to prove she was born free. Each is dated to the day by Roman consuls, and each was preserved only because the mountain buried it. They are the 'ordinary days' this book always needs — here, ordinary decades. The towns had been warned, though no one read the warning. A great earthquake around 5 February 62 (or 63 — the sources disagree) wrecked Pompeii and damaged Herculaneum; Seneca wrote a treatise on earthquakes in response, and the household of the banker Caecilius Iucundus carved the falling temple and gate onto its family shrine. Seventeen years of rebuilding followed; the election notices show a working town still arguing about its aediles. Then comes the eruption itself, seen through Pliny: his uncle the admiral sailing into the ash cloud and dying on the beach at Stabiae; the seventeen-year-old reading Livy as the house shakes, then fleeing Misenum with his mother into a darkness he likens to a sealed room with the lamp put out. Every scene of the elder Pliny is second-hand, reported by the nephew, and flagged as such. Cassius Dio, writing a century and a half later, adds giants on the mountain and a crowd caught in the theatre; Suetonius records the emperor Titus's relief commissioners. The library at the Villa of the Papyri stands for what was lost: books, not records. Even the date is contested. Pliny's manuscripts overwhelmingly give 24 August, but autumn fruit, heavy clothing and a charcoal note dated 17 October — found in 2018 in a house in Regio V — persuaded many that the eruption came on or around 24 October. The latest manuscript and experimental work has pushed back toward August. The calendar note sets out the case; the timeline places the eruption at Pliny's date and shows the October note where it falls, so readers can see both. Form tags are honest throughout: these are letters, documents, inscriptions, histories and books, not diaries. The forms are the point — an empire whose ordinary people left their dates on wax, wall and receipt, and whose one eyewitness wrote as a literary man looking back.

title: The Great Mortality
places: Piacenza, retelling events at Caffa, Crimea
Avignon (letter to the chapter of St Donatian's, Bruges)
Dublin and Drogheda, recorded at Kilkenny
Piacenza — not, it now seems, at Caffa
intro: Between 1346 and 1353 a single disease — plague, carried by the bacterium Yersinia pestis — swept from the steppe around the Black Sea through Constantinople, Egypt, Syria, Italy, France, Spain, the Maghreb, Germany and the British Isles. Perhaps a third to a half of the people in its path died. Christians called it the great mortality; Arabic writers called it the great annihilation. Neither world knew the cause, and both wrote about it. There are no diaries in the modern sense from these years. What survives is letters, chronicles, annals, medical treatises, papal bulls, a note scribbled in a beloved book, and travel memoirs dictated later. This chapter uses all of them, tagged honestly: some writers stood inside the dying city and wrote within weeks; others, like Henry Knighton, Guy de Chauliac or al-Maqrizi, looked back years or generations later; and a few famous accounts — Gabriele de' Mussi's siege of Caffa, Boccaccio's Florence — carry flags for hearsay or literary shaping. Set side by side, the Christian and Muslim witnesses rhyme more than they clash. Heyligen in Avignon and Ibn Battuta in Syria both count the dead per day and pass on numbers they could not check. Boccaccio and Ibn Khatima both see that the sick and their clothing pass the disease on. Petrarch, Ibn al-Wardi and Friar John Clyn all write knowing they may not live to finish — and in two of those cases they did not. The differences matter too. Damascus answered the plague with a procession in which Muslims, Jews and Christians walked together; much of the Latin West answered it with accusations of poisoning, and in February 1349 Strasbourg burned its Jewish community before the plague had even reached the city, despite a pope who had declared in writing that the Jews were dying like everyone else. Those events are recorded here soberly, as the chroniclers set them down. Read the timeline slowly. In the same summer of 1348, a Sienese shoemaker buries his children, a Florentine writer watches trenches fill, a Moroccan traveller prays barefoot outside Damascus, and a pope issues his first decree on the Jews. In spring 1349, an Irish friar leaves blank parchment for whoever survives, and a Syrian poet's essay ends in prayer a few days before his death. They never read one another, but they were writing the same book.

title: The Last Days of Constantinople
places: Golden Horn, watching from the boom
With the besiegers, by his account

St Demetrios sector, then in hiding

With the besiegers / in the city
Aboard the Venetian galleys in the Golden Horn and on the walls near the harbour
Inside the city during the siege
Commanding the defence near the St Demetrios sector by the Acropolis
intro: In the spring of 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II, just twenty-one, brought an army of many tens of thousands and a fleet to the walls of Constantinople. The city had been the capital of the Roman Empire in the East for over a thousand years. Now it was a shrunken place of villages and orchards inside its old walls. Its emperor, Constantine XI Palaiologos, could put together only about seven or eight thousand defenders. Fewer than five thousand of them were Greeks; the rest were Venetians, Genoese, Catalans and other outsiders. After fifty-three days of bombardment, mining, naval fights and night assaults, the city fell at dawn on Tuesday 29 May. Unlike most chapters of this book, this one has only one true diary. Nicolò Barbaro, a Venetian surgeon serving on the galleys in the harbour, wrote the siege down day by day, and his journal is the timeline everyone else hangs on. The other eyes left letters written weeks later (Leonard of Chios, Cardinal Isidore), a merchant's report (Tetaldi), an epic poem in Latin (Pusculo), a terse personal chronicle (Sphrantzes) and histories or memoirs written years or decades afterwards (Kritoboulos, Tursun Beg, Doukas, Konstantin Mihailović, Nestor Iskander). Each one carries an honest form tag. Where an entry is a narrative episode the author did not date himself, the date comes from Barbaro and the entry is marked approximate. Together they give an unusually wide spread of viewpoints on a single siege. There are Venetians and Genoese inside the walls who blamed each other. There is a Latin archbishop who blamed the Greeks for resisting Church union, and a Greek courtier who loved the emperor and lost his own children. There is a Greek islander who wrote the story for the conqueror himself, and an Ottoman secretary who watched from the sultan's side. There is a Serbian soldier sent by a Christian prince to fight for the sultan, and a Russian writer whose tale later fed Moscow's claim to be the 'Third Rome'. The book's clusters fall on the siege's turning points. 12 April: the great guns open a steady bombardment and the Ottoman fleet arrives. 20 April: four Christian ships fight their way through the whole Ottoman fleet while the sultan rides into the surf. 22 April: Ottoman ships are dragged over the hill behind Galata into the Golden Horn. 22–25 May: an eclipsed moon, a procession broken up by a storm, and a strange fog convince the defenders that heaven has turned away. 29 May: the fall, as seen from the harbour, the walls, the palace corridors, the sultan's camp and a distant island. The fall ended with a sack. Thousands were killed and many thousands enslaved, including the families of several of these writers. This chapter reports what they recorded, how many died and how they reacted, without dwelling on the violence.

title: First Contact
eyes: Anonymous Nahua authors of the Annals of Tlatelolco
Nahua elders of Tlatelolco, with Bernardino de Sahagún (Florentine Codex, Book XII)
places: La Navidad, north coast of Hispaniola
Lisbon / Florence; printed in Paris, Florence and elsewhere
Huitzillan, at the entrance to Tenochtitlan
Western mouth of the Strait of Magellan
intro: In thirty years the oceans closed into one world. In October 1492 a Genoese captain stepped onto an island in the Bahamas and met the Taíno; in November 1519 a Spanish captain met Moctezuma on the causeway of Tenochtitlan, a city larger than any in Spain; in April 1521 Magellan died in the shallows of Mactan; and in September 1522 eighteen men brought the battered Victoria home, having gone round the earth. In between, the Taíno population of the Caribbean collapsed, and the Mexica capital fell after a siege and an epidemic. This chapter must be honest about its sources. There are almost no diaries here. The European record is logs, dated letters and later memoirs: Columbus's log survives only in Bartolomé de las Casas's later abstract; Cortés's letters are legal self-defence addressed to his king; Pigafetta wrote up his journal after he got home; Bernal Díaz wrote nearly fifty years on. Some of the most quoted texts — Vespucci's printed letters above all — are disputed. The Indigenous record is later still, and that asymmetry must not be smoothed over. The Taíno left no written account at all; what we have is a friar's report of their beliefs, surviving only in Italian translation. The Nahua accounts — the Annals of Tlatelolco and Book XII of the Florentine Codex — were set down in Nahuatl a generation or more after 1521, the Annals perhaps in the 1540s and Book XII about 1555, under the eyes of friars. The people of Mactan left oral tradition, not text. Placing these sources on the same timeline as Cortés does not make them equal witnesses of the same moment; their dates are marked approximate, and their value is that they are the other side's memory, not that they are contemporaneous. The conquest was violent, and this chapter treats that soberly: what the writers recorded, the scale where it can be known, and how they justified or mourned it. Columbus noted on the day of landfall that the islanders would make good servants; Cortés described the destruction of a city he admired; the Nahua elders remembered the Toxcatl massacre, the sixty days of smallpox and the hunger of the siege. Disease, not only steel, decided much of the outcome. Then there is Europe watching. Peter Martyr at the Spanish court heard every returning captain and called it a new world within months of Columbus's return. Albrecht Dürer, in Brussels in August 1520, saw the gold sun and silver moon Moctezuma had given Cortés and wrote that nothing in his life had moved him so — weeks after the Spaniards had been driven out of Tenochtitlan and just before smallpox reached it. Read across, these eyes show wonder, greed, grief and misunderstanding happening at the same time, on different sides of the world.

title: Seven Years Across the Strait
places: On the road south after his release from prison
Southern Korea, with Ōta Kazuyoshi's troops
Usuyeong, at the mouth of the Myeongnyang strait
intro: In the spring of 1592 a Japanese army of some 150,000 men crossed the Korea Strait. Toyotomi Hideyoshi had unified Japan and meant to use Korea as a road to Ming China. Busan fell in a day, Seoul in under three weeks, and King Seonjo fled north. The war that followed lasted, with a long uneasy truce, until Hideyoshi's death in 1598. It drew in a Ming army, devastated the Korean countryside, and carried tens of thousands of Koreans off to Japan. Few early-modern wars have been written down by so many people on more than one side. On the Korean side is Yi Sun-sin's war diary, the Nanjung Ilgi, the terse private notebook of the admiral who cut Japan's sea lanes, alongside the Swaemirok of Oh Hui-mun, a stranded scholar who learned of every battle late and sometimes got it wrong. Above them both is Ryu Seong-ryong, the chief minister, whose Jingbirok was written after the war as a warning to later generations. From the invading side, the most remarkable voice belongs to Keinen, an old Pure Land priest attached to a daimyo's army, who closed each day with a poem. His diary of the 1597 campaign records burning villages, captives and children taken from their parents with a moral clarity that is rare in any army's record. Set beside him are a monk-secretary's dry log of occupied Seoul, a samurai's later war memoir from Keinen's own contingent, and the letters and seal-orders of Hideyoshi himself, who never set foot in Korea. Some of the eyes here are not diarists, and the chapter says so. Hideyoshi and the Ming superintendent Song Yingchang speak through letters and official documents. The Jesuit Gregorio de Céspedes, the first European known to have entered Korea, survives in a handful of letters. Ryu Seong-ryong, Ōkōchi Hidemoto and the captive scholar Kang Hang wrote their accounts after the events. Entries from those works are dated by the events they describe and are marked as approximate where this edition could not check the exact text. The clusters are the heart of the chapter. In the summer of 1592, Yi wins at Hansan while a Japanese monk counts storehouses in occupied Seoul and a Korean refugee hears the news eighteen days late, credited to the wrong admiral. In September 1597, Keinen and Ōkōchi describe the same storming of Namwon. In October 1597, Yi holds the Myeongnyang strait with thirteen ships while Kang Hang is taken captive off the same coast. In December 1598, Yi's last entry, Ryu's account of his death, and Oh's grief two weeks later meet at Noryang. Violence is described here as the diarists recorded it, soberly and without graphic detail. The scale was very large: Korean population and farmland took decades to recover, and the trophy noses buried in Kyoto's Mimizuka remain a site of memory today.

title: The Mandate Changes Hands
eyes: Crown Prince Sohyeon (昭顯世子) and his household diarists
places: On the road south from Shenyang
Inside Yangzhou, hiding with his family through the sack
Nanjing, then the Yangzhou front north of the Yangtze
His church and residence inside Beijing
Edo, receiving reports gathered from Chinese ship captains at Nagasaki
intro: On 25 April 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng's army walked into Beijing and the last Ming emperor hanged himself behind the palace. Within six weeks the rebels were gone too: the Ming general Wu Sangui opened Shanhai Pass to the Manchus, the combined armies broke Li on 27 May, and the Qing regent Dorgon rode into the capital on 6 June. A year later Qing armies crossed the Yangtze. Yangzhou was sacked in May 1645, Nanjing surrendered in June, and the order to shave the head and wear the queue set Jiangnan on fire that summer. Jiangyin held out for some eighty days and fell in October. The honest record of this cataclysm is not mostly diaries. Qi Biaojia's is the great exception, a daily diary kept by a Ming official for fifteen years and broken off only by his suicide in 1645. Around it this chapter sets other kinds of writing and says so: Wang Xiuchu's dated survivor's narrative of Yangzhou; the official diary kept by the Korean crown prince's retinue as they travelled with the conquering army; Shi Kefa's letters; Dorgon's edicts; the memoirs Adam Schall and Martino Martini compiled for Europe; Zhang Dai's memories written in hiding; and the Japanese shogunate's file of sailors' reports. The eyes are deliberately unlike one another. A Manchu regent and a Ming commander write to each other. A German Jesuit stays in the captured capital and sells the new dynasty an accurate calendar. A Korean prince, hostage of the Qing and loyal in spirit to the Ming, enters Beijing behind Dorgon and dies at home the day after Yangzhou falls. A Yangzhou townsman counts his dead. Two Shaoxing friends choose death and survival. A Japanese scholar's office hears of it all five months late, and his file of such reports is later named 'the transformation from civilised to barbarian'. The Yangzhou entries are treated soberly. Wang's account is a primary witness, but it is also a text with a history: suppressed under the Qing, reprinted as revolutionary propaganda, and carrying a death toll of 800,000 that historians reject. The entries give what he recorded and how he survived, not the violence in detail. Many of these writers recorded or remembered events after the fact. Where only the month or season is secure, the entry says so, and day-level content that could not be checked is described only in general terms. Read the dates as a weave of near and far: the same week looked very different from the observatory in Beijing, a garden in Shaoxing, a roof in Yangzhou, and an office in Edo.

On the Burg and Löbel bastions

intro: On 14 July 1683 Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha's army pitched its tents around Vienna, the Habsburg capital, a week after Emperor Leopold I had fled up the Danube. For sixty days about 11,000 soldiers and the city's burgher militia under Count Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg held the walls. The besiegers dug mines under the Burg and Löbel bastions, while dysentery and fire spread inside. On 12 September a relief army of Imperial, German and Polish troops under King Jan III Sobieski came down from the Kahlenberg and broke the Ottoman camp in an afternoon. This chapter sets the siege beside itself. Inside the walls are an anonymous garrison officer whose day-by-day journal was printed in London in 1684, the Imperial official Johann Peter von Vaelckeren and the city secretary Nikolaus Hocke. On the walls is the commandant himself. Kolschitzky crossed the lines and became a legend. Outside the ring are Charles of Lorraine, the Irish officer Francis Taaffe, the Capuchin Marco d'Aviano, and Sobieski and his fifteen-year-old son Jakub. On the other side of the trenches is a rare voice: the Ottoman master of ceremonies, whose campaign diary runs from the march to the Grand Vizier's execution in Belgrade. Much of the honest record is not diary in the strict sense. Sobieski, Starhemberg, Lorraine, Taaffe and Marco d'Aviano survive as dated letters and dispatches. Silahdar Fındıklılı Mehmed Ağa, who marched with the Ottoman army, wrote a chronicle afterwards. Dyakowski's 'diary' is a memoir written fifty years on. The London pamphlets are press, turning foreign letters into English news with rumour mixed in. Each eye carries its form tag, and the weaker ones are flagged in their notes. Some voices are missing, and the gaps are worth stating. No diary by a Crimean Tatar on the campaign, or by anyone in Imre Thököly's Hungarian Kuruc army, turned up in this research; the Tatars appear only through the Ottoman diarist's complaint that the khan held back. Evliya Çelebi, often quoted on Vienna, described an earlier embassy of 1665, not this siege, and is left out. The Viennese poor, the refugees and the tens of thousands of villagers killed or carried off by raiders in the countryside left no diaries that we could find. Read the clusters together. On 14 July a protocol officer and a garrison officer describe the same opening moves of a siege. On 6 September the Löbel bastion falls inside the city while the Poles cross the Danube twenty miles away. On 12 September one battle is told as a Mass, a 3 a.m. note, a teenager's itinerary, a rout, a view from the walls and a London headline.

title: The Morning the Earth Moved
eyes: Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo (later Marquis of Pombal)

intro: On Saturday 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day, at about twenty to ten in the morning, the ground under Lisbon shook in several waves over a few minutes. The churches were full for the feast. Roofs, towers and the royal palace by the river came down. Survivors ran to the open quays along the Tagus. Then the river drew back, and soon after the sea came in over the waterfront. Altar candles and kitchen fires fell into the wreckage, and by nightfall the city was burning. The fire ran for days. Nobody counted the dead reliably: witnesses in this chapter give figures from about 30,000 to 60,000, and modern estimates fall in the same broad range. This chapter has almost no diaries in the strict sense, and it says so up front. People who lived through the day mostly wrote letters: to parents, to friends, to their government, to the Royal Society. Some letters are dated the day itself, some weeks later, and one was written on New Year's Eve. Others who were far away wrote reports, official orders, essays, a poem and a sermon-tract. Each eye has a form tag that says which of these it is. Where a letter describes 1 November but was written later, the entry sits on 1 November and the date_display gives the date the letter was written. The eyes form rings around Lisbon. At the centre are three Englishmen and a Portuguese minister: the clergyman Charles Davy, who clambered over a fallen church to reach the river; the merchant Thomas Chase, pulled from his collapsed house; the surgeon Richard Wolfall, working without instruments; and Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo, the future Marquis of Pombal, writing orders from the royal camp at Belém. The British envoy Abraham Castres sheltered refugees in tents in his garden. The engineer Manuel da Maia began planning a new city within five weeks. Farther out are Madeira, where the shock and then the sea reached Funchal; Cádiz, where a wall of water broke the causeway to the mainland; and Gibraltar, where the governor gathered news from Morocco of damage at Tangier, Salé, Fez and Meknes, then of a second quake there on 18 November. The farthest ring is the strangest. Across Britain and northern Europe the ground barely moved, yet still water heaved that morning. Loch Lomond rose and fell every five minutes while an innkeeper timed it with his watch. A London fish pond emptied and overflowed. Hamburg's church chandeliers swung. In the afternoon the tsunami itself reached Cornwall and Ireland. Gentlemen sent these reports to the Royal Society, which printed dozens of them side by side in its Philosophical Transactions: in effect, the first crowd-sourced map of one earthquake's reach. Voltaire, Kant and John Wesley read the news from Geneva, Königsberg and London and drew three opposite conclusions: an indictment of easy optimism, a natural cause to be studied, and a call to repent. Some famous Lisbon material is left out or flagged. The Oratorian Father Manuel Portal's História da ruína da cidade de Lisboa is a genuine eye

title: The Sun Grew Dim
eyes: Commander of the East India Company cruiser Benares
places: Road to Dompu and Bima, Sumbawa
Makassar, Sulawesi, then at sea to Bima on Sumbawa
Sanggar, on the flank of Mount Tambora
Dompu and Bima, Sumbawa, several weeks after the eruption
Sécheron, then Maison Chapuis, Montalègre, Cologny, near Geneva
Villa Diodati, Cologny, above Lake Geneva
Geradstetten in the Rems valley, Württemberg
intro: On the evening of 5 April 1815, Mount Tambora on the island of Sumbawa began to erupt. Five days later it blew itself apart in the largest eruption in recorded history, burying the kingdoms on its slopes and sending a veil of sulphate high into the stratosphere. Tens of thousands died on Sumbawa and neighbouring Lombok, from the blast itself and then from famine and disease. The veil drifted around the world. In 1816 Europe and North America had what New Englanders came to call 'eighteen-hundred-and-froze-to-death': snow in June, frost in August, ruined harvests, and in 1817 famine across central Europe and southwest China. Almost nobody connected the cold to a volcano they had never heard of. That link was made only in the twentieth century. This chapter is honest about its sources. The eruption itself survives mostly through official reports: letters sent to Raffles by British residents and officers, and one survivor's testimony, the Raja of Sanggar's, written down by someone else. Those are compilations and relayed accounts, not diaries, and they are tagged that way. The aftermath has true diaries (a Maine farmer, a Connecticut parson, Byron's physician Polidori), alongside dated letters, a weather memorandum book, a village chronicle, poems, and one memoir written decades later. Three clusters carry the chapter. The first is the eruption, 5–12 April 1815, seen from the mountain's foot, from a warship and from Java. The second is the New England cold snap of 6–10 June 1816, logged by three men who never met. The third is the ghost-story week at Villa Diodati, 16–18 June 1816, where rain kept a group of young English writers indoors and Frankenstein and The Vampyre began. Set side by side, the eyes show a disaster that changed shape as it travelled: fire and whirlwind on Sumbawa, ash on Java, frozen washing in Connecticut, thunderstorms over Geneva, swollen feet in Württemberg, children sold in Yunnan. None of them could see the whole thing. Together they nearly do.

title: Opium and Gunboats
places: On the road west to Ili
intro: In March 1839 an imperial commissioner, Lin Zexu, reached Canton with orders to end a trade the Qing state had banned for decades and could no longer ignore. British and American merchants were importing thousands of chests of Indian opium a year, smuggled ashore with the help of Chinese dealers and officials, and silver was flowing out of China to pay for it. Within weeks Lin had the foreign factories surrounded, and Charles Elliot, Britain's Superintendent of Trade, had ordered more than twenty thousand chests surrendered to him in the Queen's name. In June Lin had the opium dissolved in trenches at Humen and let out to sea. Elliot's decision turned a police action against smugglers into a dispute between governments. Skirmishes at Kowloon and Chuanbi in late 1839 were followed in 1840 by a British expedition from India. It seized Chusan, sailed north toward Beijing, returned to fight up the Pearl River in 1841, and in 1842 forced its way up the Yangtze. The storming of Zhenjiang that July cut the Grand Canal, and on 29 August 1842 the Treaty of Nanking was signed aboard HMS Cornwallis. It opened five ports, ceded Hong Kong and imposed an indemnity of 21 million dollars. Most of the honest record here is not private diaries. Lin's diary survives; so does a townsman's diary from inside Zhenjiang. The rest are dated letters, official dispatches and edicts, missionary journalism, and officers' campaign narratives written up from journals within a year or two. Each eye is labelled with its form. Several entries are dated only to the month because the original pages could not be checked, and they are marked approx. Set side by side, these documents show how little each party could see. Lin's memorials turned skirmishes into victories for an emperor a thousand miles away. Elliot justified to London decisions he had taken alone. American merchants stayed neutral and profited. British officers wrote about fever at Chusan more than about battle. At Zhenjiang the Han townspeople feared their own Manchu garrison as much as the British, and that garrison chose death for whole families over capture. The chapter treats that ending soberly: it records what the witnesses wrote and the scale, without lingering on detail.

title: The Great Hunger
places: South Reen, near Union Hall, West Cork
London, editing reports sent in from growers
Baltiboys House near Blessington, Co. Wicklow
Cork city, travelling to and from Dublin
South Reen headland near Union Hall and Skibbereen, West Cork
Dublin, then Ulster, Donegal and Erris in Mayo
Cork to Clonakilty and Skibbereen, West Cork
Grosse Île in the St Lawrence, below Quebec
Connaught, especially Erris and Belmullet, Co. Mayo
intro: In September 1845 a mould that had crossed the Atlantic reached the potato fields around Dublin. About three million Irish people lived mainly on potatoes. Over the next seven years the crop failed again and again. Roughly a million people died of hunger and disease, and more than a million emigrated. The 1851 census counted about 1.6 million fewer people than ten years before. In Irish it is An Gorta Mór, the Great Hunger. Most of the people who suffered left no written record. Many spoke Irish and could not write, and the Irish-language diarist Amhlaoibh Ó Súilleabháin of Callan stopped writing a decade before the blight. The written record is therefore mostly made by visitors, officials and the gentry. This chapter is honest about that. Only one eye, Elizabeth Smith, kept a private diary. The rest are dated letters, editorials, official reports, an artist's dated sketches with notes, and one later narrative (Nicholson's) built from notes and letters. Each eye's form tag says which. The eyes are spread on purpose, from far to near. Lindley in London names the danger first. Trevelyan in the Treasury sets the rules of relief, and Father Mathew writes to him from Cork. Cummins and the artist James Mahony go into the Skibbereen district during the winter of 1846–47. Two Quakers, Bennett and Tuke, and the American Asenath Nicholson cross Erris in Mayo, one of the worst-affected districts. Captain Kennedy lists the evicted families of Kilrush. Across the Atlantic, Dr Douglas at Grosse Île receives the emigrant ships in 1847. The clusters show how the crisis moved from place to place: the blight news of September–October 1845, the Skibbereen winter of December 1846 to February 1847, the summer of the ships in 1847, and the clearances in Clare in 1848–50. Faraway gifts appear at their dates: the Cherokee meeting of 13 March 1847 and the Choctaw meeting about ten days later. The Ottoman Sultan's documented gift of £1,000 is real; the stories of a £10,000 offer cut to £1,000 and of secret grain ships at Drogheda are later legend. Two warnings. 'Gerald Keegan's Famine Diary', a supposed 1847 emigrant-ship journal, is fiction: it was first published as a story in 1895 and republished as a real diary in the 1980s–90s. Like Defoe in Volume I, it is named here only so readers can recognise it. 'Robert Whyte's 1847 Famine Ship Diary' reprints an 1848 book, 'The Ocean Plague', whose author cannot be identified, so it is not used as an eye either. The chapter describes suffering soberly and spares graphic detail.

title: The Black Ships
places: Anchored off Uraga, mouth of Edo Bay
Aboard USS Susquehanna, Okinawa, the Bonins and Edo Bay
Aboard USS Powhatan in Edo Bay and at Shimoda, 1854
With the squadron at Yokohama, Shimoda and Hakodate
intro: On the afternoon of 8 July 1853, four American warships — two of them steamers trailing smoke, towing the other two against the wind — anchored off Uraga at the mouth of Edo Bay. Japanese called them kurofune, black ships. For two centuries the Tokugawa shogunate had confined foreign contact to the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki. Commodore Matthew Perry had come to break that rule by refusing to obey it: he would not go to Nagasaki, would not meet minor officials, and would not leave without handing over a letter from President Fillmore. The letter changed hands at Kurihama on 14 July; Perry left on the 17th promising to return, and came back in February 1854 with a larger squadron. Talks in a hall built at the fishing village of Yokohama produced the Treaty of Kanagawa on 31 March 1854, opening Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships for supplies and rescue. It was not a trade treaty, but it ended seclusion, and within fifteen years the shogunate itself was gone. The American eyes here are unusually many, because Perry ordered every officer's journal handed over for the official history — and several men kept copies or wrote their own books. The commodore's dictated journal counts 'points' won; Samuel Wells Williams, the reluctant interpreter, is franker and more uneasy; the artist Wilhelm Heine sees mountains and larks; the journalist Bayard Taylor writes adventure; a young officer, Edward McCauley, draws; a ship's clerk, J. W. Spalding, receives a secret letter. A Chinese scholar, Luo Sen, sits between the two sides with a brush, the one man present whose own country had already been forced open by the Opium War. The Japanese record is honest but different in kind. The shogunate's response survives mostly as administrative documents — Abe Masahiro's circular asking the lords for their views, Tokugawa Nariaki's ten-point memorial for resistance, Ii Naosuke's pragmatic reply — rather than diaries, and they are tagged as such. Beside them stand the letters of Yoshida Shōin, the young samurai who watched at Uraga and then tried to stow away; the sketches of Hibata Ōsuke, a guard at Yokohama who drew the Americans for Japanese eyes; and, at Nagasaki, the diary of Kawaji Toshiakira, holding off the Russian envoy Putyatin, whose secretary Ivan Goncharov wrote his own account of the same months. The townsman's view is harder to pin to days. Edo's rumour-collectors, broadsheets (kawaraban) and satirical verses — the famous pun on 'four cups of jōkisen tea' keeping the realm awake — show panic and wit, but the individual diaries were not verified closely enough here to date; they appear in the images rather than as eyes. Read the clusters on 14 July 1853, 8–9 March 1854 and 25 April 1854 side by side: the same hours look like triumph, theatre, humiliation and opportunity depending on where one stood.

title: Delhi, 1857: The Last Mughal Summer
eyes: Mainodin Hassan Khan (Mu'in al-Din Hasan Khan)
places: Red Fort, by the river front
From the Residency to the Secundra Bagh
His house in Gali Qasim Jan, Ballimaran, inside the walled city of Delhi
His house in the walled city of Delhi, in hiding for much of the rebel occupation
Paharganj police post, then the city kotwali, Delhi
The Red Fort and the city
The British camp on the Ridge before Delhi
The Residency at Lucknow, sharing quarters with the Inglis family
Kanpur and its neighbourhood, in hiding
On the road through central India
intro: On 10 May 1857 sepoys of the Bengal Army at Meerut rose, freed their comrades who had been jailed for refusing the new greased cartridges, and rode through the night to Delhi. On 11 May they entered the city and put themselves under the 81-year-old Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, who until that morning had been a pensioner of the East India Company. Within weeks the rising had spread across the Gangetic plain. Kanpur's British garrison surrendered in June and was destroyed; the British Residency at Lucknow was besieged from 30 June; a small British army sat on the Ridge outside Delhi all summer, and stormed the city between 14 and 20 September. This chapter sets Indian and British witnesses side by side, and the record is uneven. The British side left many daily diaries, especially from the women of the Lucknow Residency, some printed within months. The Indian side left fewer: Ghalib's Persian journal and Urdu letters, a loyalist secretary's diary, the surviving issues of a Delhi newspaper, and memoirs written years or decades later by men who had reason to be careful. Several of those memoirs were shaped by fear of British retribution, and one Kanpur diary is widely doubted. Their form tags here say so plainly, and many of their entries are marked approximate. The clusters are where the voices meet. On 11 May four Delhi witnesses describe the same morning from a poet's lane, a clerk's office, a police post and the palace riverfront. On 30 June four people inside the Lucknow Residency record the defeat at Chinhat that began their siege. In early August two diarists in the Residency describe the same cannon shot. In mid-September Delhi falls, the King leaves the fort, and a British officer takes him prisoner at his ancestor's tomb. In November the Lucknow garrison walks out to the Secundra Bagh. Kanpur and the reprisals are handled soberly. Both sides killed prisoners and civilians: the British garrison and its families at Kanpur in June and July, and many thousands of Indians, combatant or not, in the British advance and the retaking of Delhi and Lucknow. The diarists record what they knew and heard. This chapter reports the events and their scale without dwelling on detail. Read together, these eyes show a war that each side saw as a betrayal. The British writers saw a mutiny by trusted servants. The Indian writers saw the end of their world: Delhi's old society scattered, its poets silenced or in exile, and its last emperor sent to Rangoon. When Ghalib writes that he is afraid to put more on paper, he is telling us why the Indian side of this chapter is quieter.

title: The Sound Heard Round the World
eyes: Mr Schruit (also printed Schuit), telegraph master at Anjer
George James Symons and the Royal Society Krakatoa Committee
American newspaper correspondents (New York, Poughkeepsie, New Haven)
places: Sunda Strait, aboard the Charles Bal
Off Sumatra, about 40 miles from Krakatoa
Aboard the Dutch vessel Prinses Marie, Sunda Strait
Roadstead of Telok Betong, Lampung Bay
Barograph stations from Calcutta to Europe
Ketimbang, on the Sumatran shore of the strait facing Krakatoa
Sunda Strait, some 10–30 miles from Krakatoa, near Button Island
Anjer, then the roadstead of Telok Betong in Lampung Bay, Sumatra
Batavia, about 160 km east of Krakatoa
Rodrigues Island, about 4,800 km west of Krakatoa
Banks of the Thames at Chelsea
intro: On 20 May 1883 a small, uninhabited volcanic island in the Sunda Strait, between Java and Sumatra, began to vent steam and ash. Ships passing through one of the busiest sea lanes of the Dutch East Indies logged the spectacle; excursion parties from Batavia even landed to look. For three months the eruption waxed and waned. Then, from about one in the afternoon of Sunday 26 August, it built into a paroxysm that ended at 10:02 on the morning of the 27th with one of the loudest sounds in recorded history. Tsunamis swept the coasts of the strait, erasing towns such as Anjer on Java and Telok Betong on Sumatra; the official toll was 36,417 dead. This chapter is unusual in the book because almost nobody here kept a private diary. The honest record of Krakatoa is a record of ships' logs, captains' reports, colonial officials' telegrams and monthly returns, scientists' instrument readings, letters to scientific journals, newspaper reports, dated pastel sketches, and one woman's account set down later. We say so plainly, and each eye carries its true form tag. Several of the best-known accounts survive mainly through two great compilations: R. D. M. Verbeek's official Dutch report Krakatau (1885) and the Royal Society's Krakatoa Committee report edited by G. J. Symons (1888). Where an entry rests on such a compilation rather than on the original document, it is flagged. The eyes are arranged by distance, because distance is the story. In the strait itself, Captain W. J. Watson of the Charles Bal and Captain Lindeman of the steamer Loudon wrote down, hour by hour, darkness at midday, pumice raining on deck, lightning playing on the masts. On the Sumatran shore, the wife of the Dutch controller at Ketimbang fled up a hill. At Anjer the telegraph master sent warnings until the line fell silent. Some 160 km away in Batavia, instruments at the observatory and a pressure gauge at the city gasworks registered the blast. Some 4,800 km away, on the small Indian Ocean island of Rodrigues, the police chief recorded what he took to be distant gunfire. Then the echo went global. The air-pressure wave from the climactic explosion was picked up on barographs in some fifty cities, passing and repassing over the globe for days; the Royal Society later gathered these traces into the first worldwide picture of a single atmospheric event. By late November 1883 the fine aerosol veil had spread around the planet, and the skies of Europe and North America burned red after sunset. A Chelsea painter sketched them in pastel by the clock; a Jesuit poet in Lancashire wrote to Nature; American fire companies reportedly turned out for blazes that were only sky. Years later Edvard Munch wrote of a blood-red sky over Kristiania, and whether that memory belongs to Krakatoa is still argued. Read side by side, these documents show something new in 1883: a disaster witnessed almost simultaneously across the world, by telegraph, by instrument and by eye, and then reassembled by scientists wh

title: Spain Divided
eyes: José Moscardó (and the El Alcázar siege bulletin)
places: Bilbao (published in London and New York)
Guernica (after its capture by Nationalist troops on 29 April)
Roof of the Poliorama cinema, La Rambla, Barcelona
Barcelona, Catalan Parliament building; written at La Pobleta
Móra la Nova, behind the Ebro
intro: On 17 and 18 July 1936 army garrisons in Spanish Morocco and then across the peninsula rose against the government of the Second Republic. In some cities the rising won within hours; in others, including Madrid and Barcelona, it was put down by loyal police and by workers' militias. What was meant to be a quick coup became a war of nearly three years, fought between the Republic and the generals who soon named Francisco Franco their leader, and drawn into the wider struggle of the 1930s by German and Italian help for one side and Soviet help and foreign volunteers for the other. This chapter sets side by side people who wrote as events unfolded or soon afterwards, from both camps and from outside. On the Republican side are the President of the Republic, Manuel Azaña, in his private notebooks; the Soviet journalist Mikhail Koltsov; and three foreign volunteers, John Cornford, George Orwell and Alvah Bessie. On the Nationalist side are Franco's own dated proclamations, the besieged garrison of the Alcázar of Toledo and its commander, the Primate of Spain, Cardinal Isidro Gomá, the German air commander Wolfram von Richthofen, and Italy's foreign minister, Galeazzo Ciano. Between and around them stand three observers: the United States ambassador, Claude Bowers; the Chilean diplomat Carlos Morla Lynch, who sheltered people from both sides in his embassy in Madrid; and George Steer of The Times. The honest record here is mixed, and the forms are labelled. Some sources are true diaries (Azaña, Koltsov, Richthofen, Bessie, Ciano, Morla Lynch). Others are dated letters (Cornford), diplomatic telegrams (Bowers), newspaper dispatches (Steer), official proclamations and communiqués (Franco), a siege bulletin (the Alcázar), church documents (Gomá) and one memoir written a few months afterwards (Orwell's Homage to Catalonia). Some diaries were reworked before they were published: Koltsov's was edited for Soviet readers in 1938 and gives some of his own doings to a figure called 'Miguel Martínez'; Richthofen's April 1937 pages were written up from shorthand notes in May. These are twentieth-century texts still under copyright, so every entry is a summary in our own words. The only quotations are three world-famous phrases. Where the two sides told the same event in different ways, as with the bombing of Guernica, the defenders of the Alcázar, or the May fighting in Barcelona, the chapter says what each source recorded and leaves the judging to the reader. Five clusters hold the chapter together: the rising and the first resistance in July 1936; the defence of Madrid in November 1936; Guernica on 26–30 April 1937; the fighting in Barcelona in May 1937 and the change of government that followed; and January–April 1939, when Barcelona fell, the President crossed into France, Madrid was occupied and the war was declared over.

title: The Notebooks Became Evidence
places: October Hall, House of the Unions, Moscow
Moscow and the writers' settlement of Peredelkino
British Embassy and the trial courtroom, Moscow
intro: In 1937 and 1938 alone, by the usual estimates drawn from the Soviet archives, the state arrested about a million and a half people and shot roughly 680,000 of them. The public face of the Terror was three Moscow show trials — Zinoviev and Kamenev in August 1936, Pyatakov and Radek in January 1937, Bukharin, Rykov and Yagoda in March 1938 — together with the secret trial and execution of Marshal Tukhachevsky and other commanders in June 1937. Its hidden mass was the 'mass operations' launched by NKVD order no. 00447 at the start of August 1937, with quotas for arrest and execution by region, which ran until the Politburo stopped them on 17 November 1938. This chapter sets diaries from inside that machine beside reports from foreigners who watched it from the courtroom gallery. Its strangest feature is that several of the diaries survive only because the police kept them. Nina Lugovskaya's schoolgirl notebooks, Andrei Arzhilovsky's peasant diary and Yulia Piatnitskaya's diary were confiscated at their arrests and used as evidence; investigators underlined the incriminating lines. They came out of the files after 1987–1991. The eyes span the whole range of belief. Georgi Dimitrov wrote down Stalin's words at the Kremlin table without comment. Maria Svanidze, part of Stalin's family circle, called the fallen chameleons months before she fell herself. Nina Kosterina promised not to pity a traitor father, then saw her father taken. Alexander Afinogenov, denounced but never arrested, used his diary to remake himself, while Stepan Podlubny tried for years to write away a kulak origin. Lyubov Shaporina in Leningrad wrote privately what few dared to think. Three foreigners frame the trials. Lion Feuchtwanger, the exiled German novelist, and Joseph Davies, the American ambassador, both found the confessions plausible; Fitzroy Maclean of the British embassy, writing a decade later, did not. Their accounts are dated letters, a travel report and a memoir rather than diaries, and are tagged that way. Davies's and Feuchtwanger's sympathy for the prosecution is flagged where it appears, not argued with. Because these are modern publications, nothing is quoted: every entry is a paraphrase. Where an exact entry date could not be checked, the date of the event is given and the entry is marked approximate. Three 'entries' are not entries at all but the day a diary was seized; they are labelled so, because in this chapter the end of a diary is part of its story.

title: The Sixth River
eyes: Louis Mountbatten, Viscount (later Earl) Mountbatten of Burma
places: Government House and Princes Park, New Delhi
East and West Punjab roads; Purana Qila, Delhi
Rahim Yar Khan to the Indian border, Bahawalpur State
Purana Qila and Humayun's Tomb camps, Delhi
Hydari Manzil, a derelict Muslim-owned house in Beliaghata, Calcutta
Mussoorie, then Delhi: Purana Qila and Humayun's Tomb camps
intro: On 3 June 1947 the Viceroy and three Indian leaders went on the radio to announce that British India would be divided. Ten weeks later, on 14 and 15 August, Pakistan and India became independent. The line between them in the Punjab and Bengal was not published until 17 August. In the months that followed, somewhere between ten and fifteen million people crossed the new borders. Hindus and Sikhs moved east, Muslims moved west and, in Bengal, people moved in both directions. Estimates of the dead run from a few hundred thousand to two million, and the violence fell on every community. The Urdu writer Fikr Taunsvi called his Lahore journal The Sixth River: the Punjab already had five rivers, and Partition added a river of blood. His is one of very few true diaries kept by an ordinary participant as events happened. Much of this chapter's record therefore comes from other forms: broadcasts and speeches by the leaders, the Viceroy's official reports, dated letters, a press attaché's diary, a photographer's essay, and memoirs written afterwards from diaries or notes. Each eye is tagged with its real form, and the later memoirs are flagged. The eyes are chosen so that each community and each new state speaks in its own voice. Nehru and Jinnah speak for the two governments, with Liaquat Ali Khan beside Nehru on the days they argued in public. Baldev Singh speaks for the Sikhs, whose homeland the Punjab line cut in two. Gandhi spends Independence Day fasting in Calcutta. Taunsvi, a Hindu, stays on in Lahore until November. Anis Kidwai, a Muslim widow, works in Delhi's camps. Penderel Moon, a British minister in a Pakistani princely state, tries to get Sikhs and Hindus out alive. Mountbatten and his press attaché watch from Government House, and Margaret Bourke-White photographs the columns going both ways. The book takes no side on the questions still argued over: who was responsible, whether the timing was right, whether the line was fair, which killings came first. Where the eyes accuse one another, as Liaquat and Nehru did in September 1947, both accusations are reported as each man made it. The violence is described by its scale and by what the witnesses did and felt, not in detail. Four clusters carry the chapter. 3 June brings the broadcasts. 14–15 August brings the midnight speeches and the celebrations, with Gandhi in a borrowed house in Calcutta. 16–17 August brings the boundary award, when every delegation found something to protest. Late August and September bring the trains, the camps, the Calcutta fast and the emergency in Delhi. Lord Wavell's journal, which ends with his departure in March 1947, falls before the period and is left out except as a link. So are novels such as Khushwant Singh's Train to Pakistan (1956) and the stories of Saadat Hasan Manto: they are powerful, but they are fiction.

title: One Small Step
eyes: Tom Reid and the Honeysuckle Creek crew
John Bolton and Neil 'Fox' Mason, Parkes Observatory
places: Columbia, atop the Saturn V, LC-39A
Eagle, descending to the Sea of Tranquillity
Foot of Eagle's ladder, Tranquility Base
Small office, Executive Office Building, Washington
Lunar Module Eagle, Tranquility Base, Sea of Tranquillity
Lunar Module Eagle and the surface at Tranquility Base
Command Module Columbia, alone in lunar orbit for about 28 hours
Mission Operations Control Room, Manned Spacecraft Center, Houston
Flight director's console, Mission Control, Houston
White House and Executive Office Building, Washington
CBS booth at Cape Kennedy for the launch
Honeysuckle Creek Tracking Station, ACT, Australia
Parkes 64-metre radio telescope, New South Wales
Jodrell Bank control room, Cheshire, England
Moscow and the cosmonaut centre at Star City
intro: Between 16 and 24 July 1969 three men flew to the Moon and back, and two of them walked on it. Few events in history were recorded so completely as they happened: every word on the radio was taped and transcribed, every heartbeat sent down as telemetry, and hundreds of millions watched live. Even so, no single record shows the whole event. The crew saw boulders Houston could not see, Houston saw numbers the crew had no time to read, and the pictures reached the world through the hands of technicians on the other side of the planet. This chapter is honest about its forms. The crew and Mission Control are heard through NASA's air-to-ground transcripts and loop recordings, which are US-government records and in the public domain, so a few of their words are quoted exactly. The Australian tracking stations are reconstructed from station records and later histories; Jodrell Bank from tapes made in its control room; Walter Cronkite from his broadcast. True diaries come from the White House (H. R. Haldeman), from Moscow (Nikolai Kamanin, the general who trained the cosmonauts), and from two English diarists who watched on television. Running underneath the American story is a Soviet one. Luna 15, a robot launched three days before Apollo 11, was meant to land, scoop up lunar soil and fly it home first. It circled the Moon while Eagle landed and crashed into the Sea of Crises two hours before Armstrong and Aldrin lifted off. Soviet television showed nothing of the landing live. The fullest account of the losing side is in Kamanin's diary, which stayed secret until the 1990s. The clusters are where to read across. On the afternoon of 20 July (UTC), Houston weighs computer alarms, Collins listens from orbit, and Australians wake to the landing with the Moon below their horizon. At 02:56 UTC on 21 July the first step happens at once late evening in Washington, the middle of the night in England and early afternoon in New South Wales. On 21 July Jodrell Bank hears Luna 15 fall silent. On 24 July a President watches the capsule come home from a ship's bridge.

title: The Wall Opens
places: Great Hall of the People, Beijing
Leipzig city centre and ring road
Zhongnanhai and the Great Hall of the People, Beijing
International Press Centre, Mohrenstraße, East Berlin
intro: In 1989 the communist systems of Central and Eastern Europe came apart within a single year, and in China a protest movement was put down by force. This chapter sets side by side the people who wrote things down as it happened: a prime minister who lost an election, a premier who ordered troops into his capital (if the diary is his), the party chief who stood against him, the aide to the Soviet leader who refused to send tanks, the West German chancellor's adviser, an East German novelist, a dissident playwright, and the diplomats whose cables are now declassified. The honest record here is mixed. True diaries exist and are published under their writers' names — Chernyaev, Rakowski, Teltschik, and the disputed text attributed to Li Peng — but much of what was written on the day was official: cables, a press conference transcript, speeches, a chronicle. Those are included with their form stated plainly. Garton Ash's essays are eyewitness reportage, not a diary. Copyright and privacy also shape the chapter: these are modern texts, so they are paraphrased rather than quoted, and only public figures and published authors appear. Two days frame everything. On Sunday 4 June 1989 Poles voted in the first partly free election in the Soviet bloc, and Solidarity won almost every seat it could contest; on the same day, hours earlier by the clock, the army cleared central Beijing. On 9 November a Politburo spokesman misread a note at a press conference, and by midnight the Berlin Wall was open. Between them come Hungary's reburial of Imre Nagy and its opening of the Austrian border (the Pan-European Picnic of 19 August, for which no published diarist is included here), Leipzig's 9 October, and after them Prague's November and Romania's December. Casualty figures for Beijing are contested and are reported here as each writer gave them. The Chinese government spoke of about 200–300 deaths including soldiers; foreign embassies and later researchers gave estimates from several hundred to several thousand; one British cable relayed a far higher figure. The chapter does not settle the question; it shows how differently it was seen from inside the Great Hall, from the diplomatic quarter, and from abroad. Read together, the eyes show how much depended on decisions not taken: troops that did not fire in Leipzig, a Soviet leadership that did not intervene, an East German official who did not know what his own paper meant. They also show how quickly each writer's hopes were overtaken — Wolf's renewed socialism, Rakowski's reform communism, Chernyaev's faith in Gorbachev's pace.
